note: 28 additional end-of-shift knowledge-check questions for Monday, to grow the pool past 40 when combined with kc-monday.json. Shape matches the Question type in src/content/types.ts (id, prompt, choices[4], answer index 0-3, why), plus beat and control ids for the coverage report. Report paths match the game: Report button, security@harborandco.com, extension 4400, callback on the number on your badge or already on file.

questions.prompt: Someone in a delivery uniform is carrying two boxes and asks you to hold the badge door. You should
choices: Hold it, since their hands are full
Let the door close and point them to reception or the buzzer
Lend them your badge for one swipe
Hold it if the uniform looks real
questions.why: A uniform and full hands are the classic tailgating setup. Reception can sign them in. The door is not yours to open for someone else.

questions.prompt: A friendly person says they work on the fifth floor and forgot their badge. The right move is
choices: Ask them a couple of questions about their team, then decide
Send them to reception for a temporary badge
Walk them up yourself
Let them in, since they knew the floor number
questions.why: Knowing a floor number proves nothing. Reception can check who they are and issue a temporary badge that is logged.

questions.prompt: You notice the stairwell door propped open with a wedge after hours. You should
choices: Leave it, but mention it next week
Prop it wider so it is noticed
Remove the wedge, let it close, and tell security
Ignore it, since someone probably needs it
questions.why: A propped door is an open entrance for anyone. Close it and report it, because someone may be relying on it to get back in.

questions.prompt: Why does a badge reader matter if the person behind you clearly works here?
choices: Each badge swipe is the record of who was inside, and access can be revoked
It does not; it only matters for strangers
Only managers need to badge
It keeps the door from wearing out
questions.why: Badges log who entered and when. Someone who quit last week may still look like a coworker.

questions.prompt: A visitor is walking the floor alone with no escort and no visitor badge. You should
choices: Confront them loudly
Take their photo and post it in chat
Assume someone invited them
Politely ask who they are meeting and walk them to reception
questions.why: A polite check and a walk to reception handles it without drama. If they refuse, tell security.

questions.prompt: The courier pulls out a card and the reader stays red. What does that tell you?
choices: The reader is broken
You should badge him in
The card is not authorized for this door
He needs to try twice
questions.why: Red means not authorized. That is the system working, not a problem for you to solve.

questions.prompt: An email signed by a senior leader asks for gift cards and says keep it quiet. The strongest warning sign is
choices: It was sent at night
It is polite
It asks for something payable and untraceable, urgently and secretly
It has a signature
questions.why: Gift cards, urgency and secrecy together are the pattern. Real leaders do not run purchases through codes in email.

questions.prompt: The display name says Elena Voss. What should you check before anything else?
choices: The font
Whether the email has a subject
Her profile photo
The actual sender address and domain
questions.why: Display names can be set to anything. The address after the @ shows who really sent it.

questions.prompt: Which action helps security the most with a suspicious email?
choices: Forwarding it to your team as a warning
Deleting it
Replying to ask if it is real
Using the Report button so it is sent with its headers
questions.why: Reporting gives security the original with headers, so they can block it for everyone. Replying confirms your address is live.

questions.prompt: You want to check whether the request is real. The safe way is to
choices: Contact the person through a channel you already know, like the directory
Call the number in the email signature
Reply to the email and ask
Wait to see if they email again
questions.why: Anything in the message may be controlled by the attacker. Use contact details you found yourself.

questions.prompt: You already bought one gift card before realizing it was a scam. Now
choices: Buy the rest so the story makes sense
Report it immediately, including the card details you sent
Keep quiet and absorb the cost
Email the sender to cancel
questions.why: Fast reporting can sometimes stop the card being cashed and warns others. Hiding it helps only the attacker.

questions.prompt: The email says I am in a meeting, do not call. Why do attackers write that?
choices: Because executives are busy
To stop you from verifying on another channel
To be polite
To save you time
questions.why: Blocking verification is the point. A request that forbids a callback is the one that needs it most.

questions.prompt: A caller from IT asks you to read back the six-digit code your phone just received. You should
choices: Read it, since IT asked
Text it instead
Read only the first three digits
Hang up and call IT on the number on your badge
questions.why: That code is the second half of your login. Real IT never needs it. Call back on a number you already trust.

questions.prompt: You get MFA approval prompts on your phone that you did not trigger. The right response is
choices: Approve one so they stop
Deny them and report to security, because someone may have your password
Ignore them
Turn off your phone
questions.why: Unexpected prompts mean someone is trying to log in as you. Deny, report, and change your password if asked.

questions.prompt: The caller knows your name, your manager and your desk number. Does that prove they are IT?
choices: No, that information is easy to gather from social media and directories
Yes, only insiders know that
Yes, if they sound confident
Only if they also know your password
questions.why: Personal details are research, not proof. Attackers build credibility before they ask.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest password practice for your work account?
choices: A short password you change monthly
Writing it on a sticky note under the keyboard
A long unique passphrase stored in the company password manager, plus MFA
The same strong password everywhere
questions.why: Length, uniqueness and a second factor matter most. Reuse means one breach opens every account.

questions.prompt: The caller says your account will be locked in five minutes unless you act now. This pressure is meant to
choices: Rush you past the pause where you would verify
Follow company policy
Test the phone line
Help you
questions.why: Artificial deadlines are a lever. A real lockout can wait the two minutes it takes to call IT back.

questions.prompt: You hung up on the fake IT call. What else should you do?
choices: Call the number back to scold them
Nothing, it is over
Post about it on social media
Report the call to security so they can warn others
questions.why: The same caller is probably working through the whole floor. One report can protect everyone else.

questions.prompt: You find a USB stick labeled Salary review in the break room. You should
choices: Plug it into a personal laptop instead
Throw it in the trash
Hand it to IT or security without plugging it in
Plug it in to find the owner
questions.why: A tempting label is bait. Plugging in an unknown device can run malicious code instantly. IT can handle it safely.

questions.prompt: Why can just plugging in a USB stick be dangerous, even without opening a file?
choices: It cannot be
It drains the battery
It voids the warranty
Some devices pretend to be a keyboard and type commands automatically
questions.why: Malicious devices can act as keyboards or network adapters the moment they connect.

questions.prompt: Why would an attacker label a drive Salary review?
choices: To be organized
Labels are random
It is a real HR file
Curiosity about pay makes people more likely to open it
questions.why: Baiting uses curiosity and emotion. The label is the lure.

questions.prompt: A coworker already plugged in the found USB. Now
choices: Restart the computer
Disconnect the computer from the network if told to, and report it to IT right away
Unplug it and say nothing
Run a scan yourself and move on
questions.why: Early reporting gives IT the best chance to contain it. A personal scan is not a substitute for the call.

questions.prompt: You need to move a work file to a colleague. The safest option is
choices: A free file-sharing site
Your personal email
The company-approved file share
A random USB stick from the drawer
questions.why: Approved channels are monitored and protected. Unknown media and personal accounts are where data leaks.

questions.prompt: Maya says Elena approved an urgent wire and the form is down. Before anything moves you should
choices: Send half now and half later
Confirm with Elena on the number finance already has on file
Email Elena at the address in Maya's forwarded message
Send it, since Maya is in finance
questions.why: Verify payment instructions on a channel you already trust. Anything in the request itself may be compromised.

questions.prompt: Which detail makes a payment request most suspicious?
choices: New bank details, urgency, and a reason the normal process can't be used
It is for a known vendor
It arrives during business hours
It has an invoice number
questions.why: Changed bank details plus a bypass of normal approvals is the signature of business email compromise.

questions.prompt: Maya is not trying to scam you. Why is refusing or verifying still right?
choices: Insiders are often pressured or fooled by an attacker posing as their boss
To get Maya in trouble
It is not; trust coworkers
Finance always lies
questions.why: The attacker is usually behind the coworker. Verifying protects Maya too.

questions.prompt: A wire was sent and now looks fraudulent. The most important next step is
choices: Report immediately so the bank can attempt a recall
Delete the emails
Wait until Monday to report
Send another wire to cancel it
questions.why: Recalls only work in the first hours. Speed matters more than anything else.

questions.prompt: Who is allowed to bypass the payment approval process in an emergency?
choices: Anyone who says it is urgent
Any manager
No one; the process is the control, especially when someone says it is urgent
Whoever has the bank login
questions.why: Attackers manufacture emergencies. The approval process exists exactly for those moments.
